itineraries.title: Fallen Empires, Sunken Waters, Rising City - 6 Day Itinerary
editorial: This is a fast itinerary involving domestic flights. If you prefer slow travel, give Mexico more time or choose one region.
What if we had more time?
We'd add Oaxaca for the food and culture, and Tulum if we wanted more Caribbean coast. Mexico can easily absorb two weeks; six days barely scratches it.

days.title: Day 1 - Mexico City
editorial: Start around the Zocalo and Templo Mayor, then spend the evening in Roma Norte.

We arrived on Independence Day and found the centre swallowed by parade crowds for hours. Even without the national celebration, CDMX's public spaces are the attraction: people spill into streets, markets and squares rather than retreating indoors.

One tiny moment stayed with us. We walked through a restaurant inside a market because it happened to connect two public spaces. Nobody cared. There is a comfort with shared space here that makes the city feel lived-in rather than policed into neat compartments.

days.title: Day 2 - Mexico City
editorial: Spend the day in Bosque de Chapultepec, Castillo de Chapultepec and the anthropology museum, then head towards Plaza Garibaldi or the historic centre in the evening.
Sunday night was particularly memorable: street performers, vendors, families and school kids were still out around 9:00 PM. CDMX is huge, but it rarely felt lonely.
Eat at Los Panchos if you can and try chiles en nogada when it is in season.

days.title: Day 3 - Teotihuacan
editorial: Make the day trip to Teotihuacan.

The pyramids are visually imposing, but the guided context makes them much more interesting: how architecture echoed the surrounding mountains and how ceremonial structures connected human life with the sky.
It deserves more attention than a quick photo stop from Mexico City.

days.title: Day 4 - Chichen Itza
editorial: Fly or travel east and devote the day to Chichen Itza and a cenote.
The Mayan cosmology is almost as memorable as the pyramid itself: sky, earth and underworld expressed through architecture, animals and agricultural cycles.
Then jump into Cenote Ik Kil. Ancient civilisation in the morning, giant sinkhole in the afternoon. Mexico is not subtle.

days.title: Day 5 - Bacalar
editorial: Bacalar is the decompression day.
The lagoon is beautiful even if you do absolutely nothing, which was fortunate because we discovered that many activities shut on Wednesday. We skipped kayaking and simply floated.
There are inexpensive private entries to shallower parts of the lagoon; when we visited, one cost 60 pesos.

We also learned that getting an Uber out of Bacalar can be difficult. A random local helped call us a cab for no reason other than kindness, which neatly summarised a lot of our interactions in Mexico.

days.title: Day 6 - Mexico City
editorial: Return to CDMX and use the final hours for whatever you missed.
Palacio de Bellas Artes did not do much for us, but tacos al pastor at El Caifan did. Choose accordingly.
One practical lesson: taxis were two to three times the cost of Uber during our trip, a discovery we made by paying tuition to the school of life.
